Today we'll be working with data from Csárdi et al. on the relationship between protein and RNA levels in yeast <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1005206>.
We'll build a linear model to examine the relationship quantitatively.

First, we load `tidyverse` and `mlr`.
```{r echo=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(mlr)
```

Download the data file from Content -> Datasets -> ProteinRNAlevels. It's stored in tab-separated-value format, with comment lines that begin with `#`, so we use the following function to read it in. We will keep the mRNA and protein level measurements and remove any observations with NAs.
```{r message=FALSE}
df <- read_tsv("scer-mrna-protein-absolute-estimate-sample.txt", comment="#")
df <- df %>% select("mrna","prot") %>% drop_na()
```

### Problem 3: Whiteboard question

Now we'll fit our linear model, using the `lm` function. The syntax below says that the variable `logprot` depends linearly on the variable `logmrna`. (R automatically adds an intercept term to the model.)
```{r}
mod <- lm(logprot ~ logmrna, data=df)
```

To see details about the fit, use
```{r}
summary(mod)
```

***What is the estimated slope of the relationship? Is it significantly different from 1? How can you tell? (Hint: use a 95% confidence interval) What does that mean about the relationship between mRNA and protein levels?*** Insert a photo of your work here.

```{r, eval=F, echo = FALSE, out.width = "600px"}
knitr::include_graphics("YourDrawing.jpg")
```


### Problem 4

To examine the linear fit in more detail, we'll carry out the same linear regression using the `mlr` package. The following code will allow you to create the task with `logprot` as the target, make a univariate regression learner using `regr.lm`, and train the model on the task.

```{r}
df_mlr <- df %>% select(starts_with("log"))
rnaTask <- makeRegrTask(data = df_mlr, target = "logprot")
lmLearner <- makeLearner("regr.lm",predict.type="se")
lmrna <- train(lmLearner, rnaTask)
```

Next, we want to plot model predictions on the same plot as the data.
First, let's calculate the predictions. We will create a grid of equally spaced logmrna values, make predictions using the previously determined linear model, and place the values into a new data frame called `grid`. 
```{r}
x_grid <- data.frame(logmrna=seq(from=min(df$logmrna),to=max(df$logmrna),length.out=100))
y_grid <- predict(lmrna, newdata=x_grid)
grid <- data.frame(logmrna=x_grid,pred=y_grid$data$response)
```

Make a point plot of `logprot` vs `logmrna` with a red line showing the model predictions.
```{r}

```

(Hint: For the line, use `geom_line` and the `grid` data frame.)

***Visually, how well does a line fit these data?***

### Problem 5

As a more sensitive visual test, we can plot the residuals.
To calculate them, use `residuals(mod)` and create a new `resid` column in our data frame.
```{r}
df <- df %>% mutate(resid=residuals(mod))
```

***Why do we create a new data frame for the model predictions, but add the residuals to the original data frame?***

Now make a point plot of the residuals versus `logmrna`.
```{r}

```

***From the residual plot, what can we conclude about the fit of our model to the data?***

### Problem 6

Recall from class that $r^2$ quantifies how much of the variance in the data is accounted for by our model. We can access it from our model output using
```{r}
summary(mod)$r.squared
```
And also recall that we expect $r^2$ from the linear model to be equal to the square of the Pearson correlation coefficient.
You can calculate the Pearson correlation coefficient using the following.
```{r}
cor(df$logmrna, df$logprot)
```

***Do our two methods of calculating $r^2$ agree?***
